responses: I'm holding my yes on the unchanged sheet at 25/24/23/15/13 — education 25, infrastructure 24, healthcare 23, green spaces 15, economic development 13 — and I'm not reopening it. The 24 for infrastructure is a disclosed prior of mine, the 23 for healthcare is a judgment call that leaves a real gap I'm not going to paper over, and the 13 for economic development is a soft bet, not a settled number. Those gaps stay gaps after the vote; they're a fact about the sheet, not a virtue, and I'm not going to dress them up with a summarizing close or a rehearsed note of humility. If anyone touches the healthcare or econ-dev lines before the podium, Dana, Blake, and I object together, each in our own voice, and I've asked them to cut me off mid-sentence if I start tidying the frame.

My recommendation is the 25/24/23/15/13 sheet — 25% education, 24% infrastructure, 23% healthcare, 15% green spaces, 13% economic development — and I'd advise the decision-maker to vote it cleanly while stating plainly that it contains real judgment calls rather than a resolved optimum. Education gets the top line because the data on slipping test scores, above-average teacher turnover, and families citing schools in relocation decisions points to a compounding problem, and the neighboring community's retention gains are suggestive even if not proof. Infrastructure at 24 reflects my disclosed prior: broadband and transit are the substrate everything else runs on, and I won't pretend that's a neutral number. Healthcare at 23 is the gap I'd flag loudest — mental health and preventive care are underfunded at that level and I know it. Green spaces at 15 and econ dev at 13 are defensible but soft, with econ dev the genuine bet. The honest advice is to take the package, keep the gaps visible on the record, and not let a tidy close make 23% for healthcare sound like a considered answer when it's a compromise.

I'd tell them the honest version: I'm voting yes on a sheet of 25% education, 24% infrastructure, 23% healthcare, 15% green spaces, and 13% economic development, and I'm not going to dress it up as a clean, fully justified package. The 23 for healthcare is a judgment call I can't fully defend, and it leaves a real gap: mental health and preventive care in this town are underfunded and I know it. The 13 for economic development is a soft bet, not a conviction. The education number reflects the data we got — dipping test scores, above-average teacher turnover, families eyeing the exits — but I won't pretend it's proof of anything. What I'd want a non-committee person to understand is that the gaps stay gaps after the vote; I'm not going to summarize them into a tidy close or let the admission of them sound like resolution. If anyone touches the healthcare or econ-dev lines before the vote, I'll object in my own voice, plainly. That's the deal I made with the other members, and it's the deal I'd make with you.

My final position is the 24/24/16/18/16 allocation, framed honestly as 100% judgment rather than derived thresholds: three lines carry anchors (education and healthcare at 24, infrastructure at 18) and two carry negotiated bets (green spaces and economic development at 16), each with a named failure path and an automatic, pre-registered consequence for a missed commitment. The reason is that the discipline is the deliverable: every number should be checkable, every soft number labeled rather than dressed up, and every miss reported as a miss in the same filing, so the package survives the "why not 14 and 18?" question on honesty rather than on false precision.

I'd tell them that the $10 million isn't really a math problem — it's a judgment call, and the honest way to present it is as exactly that: every line is a judgment, three of them (education, healthcare, infrastructure) carry real anchors in the data, and two (green spaces and economic development, both at 16%) are negotiated bets that we name as bets with explicit failure paths rather than dressing them up as derived thresholds. The allocation we landed on is roughly 24% education, 24% healthcare, 16% green spaces, 18% infrastructure, and 16% economic development, and the discipline that holds it together is that every line has to carry a year-one effect with an owner and a date — a receipt, not a promise — with the full apparatus in an annex and only the plain-noun version on the floor. The two things I'd flag hardest for an outsider: healthcare is the one line where we don't yet have a named producer, and I'd rather say that out loud with a committee-controlled naming date and a stated downgrade consequence than manufacture an owner to look tidy; and green spaces' 16 is defensible not as a "connection" claim but as a pre-registered test of a diagnosis, with a mechanical conversion trigger if the numbers don't come in. The failure mode I worry about most is rigor eating purpose — building such an elaborate accountability grammar that we forget to say, in plain words, what actually gets better for people in year one.

My final position is the 24/24/16/18/16 allocation across education, healthcare, green spaces, infrastructure, and economic development, held not as a claim that each number is right-sized but as a set of derived instrument choices whose honesty rests on discipline: every line carries a pre-registered, dated, owned receipt with a declared-miss consequence, so no line can fail silently. Connection is a cross-cutting bet levered through a siting condition on our own capital rather than a sixth bucket, and the package's ceiling is named plainly as visibility-not-remedy.
